beats.intro: Alternative investments, module four. [[sub]]Real estate and infrastructure: tangible assets that produce income, and sit between bonds and equities.
beats.sectors: [[a]]Real estate is land and buildings. [[res]]Residential property, the housing market, is by far the largest sector, over seventy-five percent of global real estate value. [[com]]Commercial property includes offices, shopping centers, warehouses, and rental housing owned by investors. [[feat]]Real estate is unusual. Every property is different, so it is heterogeneous. The initial outlay is large. Markets are local and fragmented. Prices are hard to discover, because trades are infrequent and history may not reflect today. And transaction costs are high.
beats.forms: [[a]]Investors can own property directly, or indirectly. [[dir]]Direct ownership brings control over tenants, leases and spending, tax benefits from depreciation and interest, and diversification. [[dis]]But it is complex, needs specialized local knowledge, and a lot of capital. It concentrates risk, and it is illiquid, with high costs. [[ind]]Indirect routes pool investors' money: real estate funds, limited partnerships, joint ventures, listed shares, and real estate investment trusts. [[debt]]Debt investors lend through mortgages, or buy mortgage-backed securities.
beats.reit: [[a]]A REIT is a tax-advantaged trust that owns, operates, and sometimes develops income-producing property. [[tax]]Its main appeal is avoiding double taxation. It pays no corporate tax if it distributes ninety to one hundred percent of its taxable net rental income. [[types]]Equity REITs own properties. Mortgage REITs lend or hold mortgage-backed securities. Hybrid REITs do both. [[ffo]]Equity REITs report funds from operations, which adjusts earnings for depreciation, to better estimate dividends. [[pro]]Listed REITs give transparency, liquidity, and professional management. The downside is a higher correlation with equity markets than private real estate. [[core]]Open-end funds hold well-leased property in the best markets: core real estate, with stable income. Investors who accept development and repositioning risk for higher returns use closed-end funds.
beats.spectrum: [[a]]Real estate spans a spectrum of risk and return. [[sd]]At the bottom, senior debt: first mortgages. Bond-like. [[core]]Core: stable, income-producing properties, such as long leases, or sale-leasebacks. Returns come mainly from lease payments. [[plus]]Core-plus: some refurbishment and tenant repositioning. [[va]]Value-add: leasing vacant space, redevelopment. Returns turn increasingly equity-like, with price appreciation. [[opp]]Opportunistic: development and distressed properties. The highest return potential, with regulatory risk, construction delays, and cost overruns. [[lev]]Leverage magnifies gains and losses at every level.
beats.income: [[a]]More than half of the return to commercial real estate investors comes from income. The rest is long-term price appreciation. [[cons]]Income, mostly from multi-year leases, is a more consistent source of return across a market cycle than appreciation. That makes real estate somewhat like a convertible bond: steady cash flows, with the chance of capital gains. [[infl]]Regular rent adjustments also give some inflation protection, though this varies by location and period. [[ltv]]Leverage creates covenants. A fund owes seventy million pounds on properties that have fallen to ninety-two million. Loan to value is point seven six, above the agreed point seven five, so the fund must add about one point three million pounds of collateral.
beats.divers: [[a]]Real estate has historically had low to moderate correlation with other assets. [[tab]]Private real estate correlates about point five with the S and P five hundred, and point four six with world equities. Real estate debt is point four, and point three eight. [[reit]]But in steep downturns, such as two thousand eight, listed REIT correlations with equities rise. [[smooth]]And private real estate is appraised perhaps once a year, while REITs trade continuously. That mismatch in valuation timing makes private correlations look artificially low.
beats.infra: [[a]]Infrastructure assets are capital intensive, long-lived, and provide essential services: transport, utilities, communications, and social facilities. [[cf]]Cash flows come from contracts, not leases. Availability payments, for keeping a facility available. Usage-based payments, such as tolls. And take-or-pay arrangements, where buyers must pay for a minimum volume. [[ppp]]Governments own most infrastructure, but increasingly use public-private partnerships, and work with development finance institutions. [[eco]]Economic infrastructure includes transportation, such as roads, ports and airports; information and communication assets, such as towers and data centers; and utilities and energy. [[soc]]Social infrastructure covers schools, hospitals, social housing, and prisons, usually paid through availability payments.
beats.stages: [[a]]Infrastructure is also classified by stage. [[green]]Greenfield: building new assets. The riskiest, with the highest expected return. It follows a build-operate-transfer life cycle. [[bot]]Build: long approval and construction, negative cash flow. Operate: under a concession agreement, the investor earns income on agreed terms. Transfer: the asset passes to the government, is sold, or is decommissioned. [[brown]]Brownfield: expanding an existing facility, or buying a privatized asset. Shorter horizon, with immediate cash flows and an operating history. [[sec]]Secondary stage: fully operational assets needing no further development. Steady, bond-like cash flows, the lowest risk, and the lowest return.
beats.forms2: [[a]]Infrastructure investors can go direct or indirect. [[dir]]Direct investment gives control, but needs large capital and brings concentration and liquidity risk. So it is often done by consortia, and by large pension and sovereign wealth funds. For example, Canada Pension Plan paid about two hundred seventy million Canadian dollars for a forty-five percent stake in Iguá, a Brazilian water and sewage company. [[ind]]Indirect routes include infrastructure funds, ETFs, listed infrastructure companies, and master limited partnerships, which are pass-through entities common in energy transport. Listed infrastructure is liquid and transparent, but a small segment of the market. [[debt]]Infrastructure debt can be private, or traded, with flexible terms to handle years of zero cash flow.
beats.returns: [[a]]Risk and return depend on the type, stage, and location. [[prof]]High-risk greenfield projects without guaranteed demand target equity returns of fourteen percent or more. Medium-risk mostly brownfield assets target ten to twelve percent. Low-risk brownfield assets with contracted revenues target six to eight percent. Most funds gravitate to the medium and low profiles, averaging around ten percent. [[stats]]Historically, private infrastructure returned eight point five seven percent a year with a standard deviation of seven percent. That is a coefficient of variation of point eight two, much better than real estate or natural resources. [[corr]]Its correlation with the S and P five hundred was just point one two, and with world equities point oh eight. Infrastructure provides income, diversification, and some protection against inflation and GDP swings.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Real estate is heterogeneous, local, and illiquid, owned directly or through funds and REITs. [[w2]]Returns run from bond-like to equity-like, and income is more than half of the total. [[w3]]Infrastructure earns contractual cash flows, and greenfield, brownfield and secondary stages trade risk for return. [[w4]]Both offer diversification, but listed real estate behaves more like equities in a crisis.
beats.finish: Module four complete. Next: natural resources.
